procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Subordinate Judge, Asansol
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated April 6, 1950, of the Calcutta High Court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Calcutta High Court affirmed the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Judge of Asansol dated June 30, 1943, in Title Suit No. 2 of 1942.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The defendants, Sumitra Devi (widow of Ram Kishori Lal) and Kamala Devi (daughter of Ram Kishori Lal), appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and decree of the Calcutta High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and remanded the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the deed of gift executed by the widow (defendant No. 1) in favour of her daughter (defendant No. 2) was valid and binding on the reversioners (plaintiffs) beyond her own lifetime.
appellant_arguments: The appellants likely argued that the deed of gift was valid and within the widow's power to execute.

The text indicates the appellants' counsel made a two-fold argument, which likely included the contention that the Hindu Succession Act, being retrospective in effect, enlarged the widow's limited estate into an absolute one, thereby validating the gift.
respondent_arguments: The widow (defendant No. 1) was not competent under the law to make the gift, as she only had a life interest in the property.
The gift was not for any justifying legal necessity and therefore could not be operative beyond the widow's lifetime or be binding on the reversioners.
The portion of the estate gifted as a marriage dowry was unreasonably large.
The gift was collusive, fraudulent, and without consideration.

cases.principle: No hard and fast rule could be laid down to define the extent and limit of the widow's power of disposing of the property inherited by her for the marriage of her daughter.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Hindu father is competent to make a gift of a reasonable portion of the ancestral immovable property to his daughters. Such a gift is binding on the joint family if, having regard to the state of the family at the time of the gift, the extent of the family property, and its indebtedness, the gift can be held to be reasonable. A gift made long after the marriage may be supported on the ground that it fulfils a moral or religious obligation.
obiter: Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is retrospective in effect by reason of the use of the expression 'whether acquired before or after the commencement of this Act'.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A Hindu widow in possession of her deceased husband's estate can validly alienate a reasonable portion of that property by making a gift to her daughter. Such a gift, even if made after the marriage, is considered a pious act that confers spiritual benefit upon the deceased husband and is justified by the continuing moral and religious obligation of the family to provide a marriage portion for the daughter.
legal_tests_applied: Pious Purpose Test: A widow can alienate property for religious acts that are not essential or obligatory but are pious observances which conduce to the bliss of the deceased husband's soul.

Reasonableness Test: For pious acts, as distinguished from essential or obligatory acts, the alienation must be of a 'reasonable portion of the property.' The reasonableness depends on the facts and circumstances of each case, including the state of the family, the extent of the property, and family indebtedness.

Continuing Moral Obligation Test: The moral obligation of a family to provide a marriage portion for a daughter does not end at the time of the marriage and can be fulfilled by a gift made afterwards.
why_respondent_won: The court rejected the argument that a widow's power is strictly limited, finding instead that she can alienate a reasonable portion of the property for pious purposes that confer spiritual benefit on her deceased husband.

The court determined that a gift to a daughter as a marriage portion is a recognized pious act under Hindu law, which does not require the stricter standard of 'sheer legal necessity' that would be needed to alienate the entire estate.

The court found, based on a review of case law, that a gift to a daughter does not have to be made at the time of the marriage but can be validly executed afterwards in fulfillment of a promise or a continuing moral obligation.

The court affirmed the principle that gifts of landed property by a widow to her daughter or son-in-law in connection with a marriage are well-recognized, thus overriding the respondent's contention that the widow was incompetent to make such a gift.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning is heavily based on the 'imperative religious duty and a moral obligation' under Hindu law for a father, mother, or guardian to give a girl in marriage and provide for her.
The justification for the widow's power to alienate property is linked to the spiritual welfare of the deceased, as such pious acts are believed to 'conduce to the bliss of the deceased's soul.'

The recognition that a moral obligation to provide a marriage portion continues until it is fulfilled reflects a policy of ensuring that daughters are not deprived of their provision from the family estate simply due to the timing of the gift.
